title: Construction Contract Price Types: Lump-Sum, Unit-Price, Adjustable
desc: Lump-sum, fixed unit-price, adjustable unit-price and other construction contract price types under Decree 210/2026/ND-CP, and which to pick for a house.
summary: The nine contract price types under the Construction Law 2025 and Decree 210/2026/ND-CP, when each applies, and suggestions for choosing the right one when building a house.
body: Even among "house construction contracts", the way payment is calculated can differ greatly. Clause 2, Article 82 of the Construction Law 2025 divides contracts into 9 types by price form; Article 6 and Article 11 of Decree 210/2026/ND-CP explain each type and when to use it.

The price is fixed at signing and does not change throughout the contract, corresponding to the agreed scope of work, quality, and schedule; it changes only in cases of force majeure, a fundamental change of circumstances, a change in the scope of work, or other cases the parties agree (Point a, Clause 2, Article 6).

Suitable when quantities and unit prices are clearly defined and unlikely to change (Point a, Clause 3, Article 11). This is the common form for "turnkey" house construction: the homeowner knows the total cost in advance, and the contractor bears the quantity and price risk within the agreed scope.

The unit price of each item of work does not change, but payment is calculated on the actual quantity accepted (Point b, Clause 2, Article 6). Used when the scope of work is clear and the risk of price fluctuation is low but the quantity is uncertain (Point b, Clause 3, Article 11), for example foundation excavation or ground reinforcement where the exact quantity is not yet known.

Unit prices and the contract price may be adjusted as agreed for all of the work (Point c, Clause 2, Article 6). Used when the conditions are not yet sufficient to determine the risk of price fluctuation; the adjustment method and price escalation contingency are agreed by the parties (Point c, Clause 3, Article 11). Common in projects with a long construction period.
Time-based: paid at hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly rates; often used for consulting services (Point d).
Cost-plus-fee: actual direct costs plus the contractor's management costs and profit (Point đ).
Output-based: payment according to the quantity and quality of accepted output products (Point e).
Percentage-based: the price is calculated as a percentage of cost or of the value of the work; often used for consulting and insurance (Point g).
Mixed: a combination of several forms for different parts of the work (Point h).
Other construction contracts: a price form agreed by the parties apart from the types above (Point i).
5. Which type should you choose for building a house?

Full drawings available and materials fixed: a lump-sum contract lets the homeowner control the total cost. It should be accompanied by a bill of quantities and a materials specification, and should state clearly the cases in which adjustment is allowed.
Underground works, or renovation work where quantities are hard to predict: a fixed unit price for that part, paid on the actual quantity measured and accepted.
Combination: the superstructure on a lump-sum basis and the foundation or finishing on a unit-price basis, i.e. a mixed contract.

Whichever type is chosen, the contract should state clearly which costs, taxes, and fees are included in and excluded from the price (Clause 2, Article 11). For contracts of public investment and PPP projects, a lump-sum contract is paid by the percentage of the contract price for each stage, without detailed quantity confirmation (Point c, Clause 4, Article 28).
To fix a lump-sum price, the homeowner needs full drawings; see Designing your own house in 2026: when must you hire a design firm?.

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace legal documents. "Commonly applied" in Decree 210/2026/ND-CP is guidance; the choice of price form for a private house is agreed between the homeowner and the contractor.
